analysis.one_liner: Requires hospitals and health insurers to publish their actual prices, including negotiated rates, so patients can see costs in advance.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in January 2023, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health Subcommittee, and never received a vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every hospital to post a public, plain-language list of its charges — including the rates it secretly negotiated with each insurer, its discounted cash price, and prices for at least 300 services patients can schedule in advance, with a free online tool to look them up. It would also have required health plans to publish what they pay in-network and out-of-network doctors and hospitals and what they pay for prescription drugs, and to give members a free tool that estimates what a specific service would cost them out of pocket. It died in committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and anyone who pays for health care. The bill would have let people see, before getting care, what a hospital charges, what it accepted from each insurer, and what it charges someone paying cash — useful for the uninsured and self-pay patients especially. Insured patients could have used a free tool to estimate their actual out-of-pocket cost for a scheduled service, instead of getting a surprise bill afterward. Employers buying coverage for workers would also have gained visibility into what their plans pay providers.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients and employers paying for care

how_it_helps.text: Requires every hospital to publish, free of charge and in plain language, its gross charges, the specific rates it negotiated with each insurer, its highest and lowest negotiated charges, and its discounted cash price.

Requires hospitals to disclose prices for at least 300 'shoppable services' — things a patient can schedule in advance — or maintain a free online estimator tool that shows what the patient would actually owe, searchable by service, billing code, and insurer, without giving personal information.

Requires health plans to publish in-network and out-of-network rates and the negotiated prices for covered prescription drugs, and to provide a free online tool where consumers can look up what a specific service would cost them under their plan, including their deductible and cost-sharing status, plus a paper option on request.
Extends these disclosure requirements to all group health plans, including self-insured employer plans, not just plans sold on the ACA exchanges.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals and health insurers. They would have had to compile and publish extensive price data in machine-readable, consumer-friendly formats, maintain online price-estimator tools, and in hospitals' case face a civil penalty of up to $300 per day for failing to comply. Beyond compliance costs, public disclosure of negotiated rates would have exposed the wide price differences among insurers and weakened their bargaining positions.

drawbacks.text: The enforcement is weak: a hospital that refuses to publish its charges faces a penalty capped at $300 per day — at most about $110,000 a year — which for a large hospital system can be less than the cost of hiring a single compliance employee, giving hospitals little financial reason to comply if they prefer not to.

Transparency alone does not guarantee lower prices. Patients usually cannot shop for emergency or inpatient care, and disclosing the lowest negotiated rates can let hospitals see what competitors have agreed to accept, which some health economists argue can push prices up rather than down during contract negotiations.

Hospitals and insurers bear real compliance costs — maintaining 300 shoppable-service price files or online estimator tools and real-time cost-sharing lookups — and supporters should acknowledge that small hospitals with thin margins may find these requirements heavier than large systems do.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On the merits, the bill's benefits — real prices in plain language, free search tools, and a cash price that lets uninsured and self-pay patients comparison-shop — outweigh modest compliance costs, and its main honest weakness is design: a $300-per-day penalty is small enough that large hospital systems could treat it as a cost of doing business, and transparency by itself does not force prices down. It died without a vote, so none of these tradeoffs were ever tested in Congress.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in January 2023, sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee, and stayed there with no hearing or vote until the two-year session ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Rep. Warren Davidson (R-OH) on January 20, 2023 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
A week later, on January 27, 2023, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, which is where action stopped.
No further action was taken — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 without the bill moving.
The bill attracted two cosponsors, both Republicans, and never expanded beyond that.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals and health insurers are better off: they never had to put their negotiated rates, cash prices, and drug costs into public, searchable files, so the pricing information patients and employers could see remains whatever current rules require.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospitals and insurers, who avoided new price disclosures

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so there is no record of where members stood; the sponsor and both cosponsors were Republicans, though hospital price transparency has drawn bipartisan interest nationally.

industries.note: Hospitals would have to publish their chargemaster prices, the rates they negotiated with each insurer, and their cash discounts for at least 300 schedulable services. Exposing the wide gaps between what different insurers pay (and what cash patients are charged) invites comparison shopping and harder rate negotiations. The bill's $300-a-day penalty cap, however, is small for most hospital systems.

Insurers would have to disclose in-network and out-of-network rates and drug prices, and build free real-time cost-estimator tools for members. Published negotiated rates would erode the secrecy that limits price competition among plans and gives members the data to question out-of-network bills.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and drug-price intermediaries
industries.note: Plans would have to publish the 'historical net price' of covered drugs — the average amount actually paid after rebates, discounts, and fees are accounted for. That would pull back the curtain on rebate deals that PBMs and insurers currently do not have to reveal.
